The recovering parser on a Livelit Playground slide: 452 s for full-body.hz. Found under ^ticket(4): the editor's recovering parser (Parser.to_segment, segmented, but a slide is one long let ... in chain) is near-quadratic there. MenhirCorpus per file on a laptop: full-body 452 s, shoes 386, scenes 210, emotion-kids 178, witch 169; 2096 s for the playground, about 5 min of it when CI was green. ReparseDocSlides and TextRoundtrip.DocSlides parse the same slides again. If Matthew takes the gate (^ticket(4), local commit f953119482: over 25 KB, only in the weekly run), this is what brings them back per PR. Known leads from the 2026-09-28 profile: Insert.go per character re-molds the whole sibling run; Form.try_get is 12% (a cheap memo); GC 41%. Tried 2026-10-14 night: local commit 0825830190 (branch parser-get-base-memo in ~/hazel-ci-heap, on ci-heap-4-pick, not pushed) keeps each label's molds in Form.Molds.get_base and runs the atomic regexes once instead of up to three times. MenhirCorpus on eyes.hz, alternating runs: 90.1 and 84.6 s before, 75.4 and 72.5 s after, about 15% faster; the parse still matches Menhir and the quick suite passes. Not enough to drop the 25 KB gate (it would take the playground's 2096 s to about 1800); the per-character re-mold of the whole sibling run is the real cost.

The commit path: find which of the request's values are new (about 15 ms of hashing, profiled), and make the commit's redraw cheaper. Part done, 2026-10-14, in node on #2635 at 41897ec3a5 (probe 4f0e261652, branch request-hash-probe in ~/hazel-ci-heap-2635, local only): a release-like edit (one literal, ids kept) through the app's own path, six edits each, steady state. Statics after the edit (DefStatics, per item): 25–37 ms. Only about 5% of the request is new objects: Kids' Choice 2,039 of 40k program nodes and about 4,600 of 87k EvalInfo nodes; Full Body 396 of 196k and about 13,100 of 326k. Building the request: the EvalInfo projection is the largest part, 13–14 ms on Full Body and 2.5–9 ms on Kids' Choice, because project_from walks both whole statics maps in key order on every commit, though about 180 entries change; then hashing the new values about 1–4 ms, and encoding 1.5–5 ms. So the hashing is not the cost. Tried and dropped: keeping an entry that is equal by content (ValueHash) as well as by identity: Full Body's re-added entries 179 to 30 and its EvalInfo new nodes 13,100 to 2,200, but the whole request got slower (median about 20 ms against 17), since comparing by content hashes as much as it saves. Done and pushed to #2635, 2026-10-14: 043508921b (DefStatics hands EvalInfo the keys it touched; the projection updates only those) and 9fb2bdf067 (unchanged spine roots kept): on Full Body the request 15.5–18.8 → 2.5–3.0 ms, statics after the edit 25–31 → 16–20 ms. Carrying it to diverged branches is ^ticket(47) (^report(13)). The commit's redraw, the ticket's second half, is not started.

Option B from ^report(5): evaluate each livelit's view in the worker, keep the last Html sent per livelit, and post patches to it, so view evaluation leaves the main thread. Needs the view runner (ViewCmdRunner) in the worker, a patch format, an element on the page that owns each livelit's DOM and applies patches, and handlers dispatched by id. Keep the page's own path for an interaction's immediate redraw, or every drag waits a round trip. Its condition is now met (2026-10-12, see ^ticket(10)): evaluating the view is about 69% of the main thread in a woods figure move, and C would save about 2%. Weigh it against making the view itself cheaper first (^ticket(1), ^ticket(2)).

Budgets harder to fool (^report(6)'s update, a count is not a time): count the call memo's own work (the nodes its keys put in form) and, if js_of_ocaml can report it, memory allocated, beside the evaluator's steps.

UX mode re-elaborates an open cell's item with fresh ids on every change (the drawn cell in ^report(8)'s B), so its parts never match by hash and fall to the reuse check's slow path. Keep the ids stable when a cell is analyzed again.

From ^ticket(45), which measured it and ruled out every cache and table (its outcome, and the work notes of 2026-10-14). The holder is not a table: it keeps whole versions of the editor's state. A heap snapshot would name it, but snapshots kill this page's renderer (snap Chromium and Chrome for Testing 155 alike, with the hang monitor off; a trivial page and a million-deep chain of arrays are fine). Lead: a page with a WeakMap of 2 million live entries did not finish its snapshot in 400 s, and ValueHash's memo is a WeakMap of about that size: try a probe build with ValueHash's memo off (or bounded), and take the snapshots then. Serve matthewhammer.org over HTTPS. Today https://matthewhammer.org/ fails: it presents GitHub's own certificate (*.github.com, Sectigo), not one for matthewhammer.org, so browsers warn and agents' fetches fail; everything is linked as HTTP. The blocker, checked 2026-10-14: the apex A record still points at 192.30.252.153, GitHub Pages' address from before 2018. GitHub serves the site there over HTTP but will not issue a certificate for a domain pointed at it; the Pages settings have no certificate and https_enforced: false. www is fine: a CNAME to matthewhammer.github.io, on the current addresses. The domain's nameservers are ns-cloud-c1..c4.googledomains.com (Google Domains, now Squarespace Domains), so the DNS change is Matthew's, in his registrar's account. Steps: (1) Matthew replaces the apex A record with GitHub Pages' four, 185.199.108.153, 185.199.109.153, 185.199.110.153, 185.199.111.153 (and may add the four AAAA, 2606:50c0:8000::153 to 8003::153); (2) once that resolves, GitHub provisions a certificate for the custom domain, which can take up to a day (re-saving the custom domain in the homepage repo's Pages settings restarts it if it stalls); (3) turn on Enforce HTTPS for the homepage and the project sites under it (hazel-work-notes, kids-choice-games); (4) check every page for mixed content: anything a page loads by an absolute http://matthewhammer.org/ URL (the series' live hover cards read report pages; the dashboard's cards too) is blocked from an HTTPS page, so make those relative or HTTPS; (5) switch the links we publish to HTTPS: READMEs, the series' agent instructions ("HTTP only"), the dashboard, the reports, #2609's ^report links; old HTTP links keep working, since GitHub redirects them once HTTPS is enforced. Progress, 2026-10-14 afternoon: Matthew changed the apex A record in Squarespace to 185.199.108.153; the authoritative nameservers and public resolvers (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1) answer it, while this laptop's resolver still had the old address cached (TTL 1 hour). GitHub has not issued a certificate yet (https_certificate: null). Still to do: the other three A records (.109, .110, .111) for redundancy, and re-saving the custom domain in the homepage repo's Pages settings so GitHub checks DNS again and issues the certificate. Later that afternoon: the new address had reached Google's, Cloudflare's and Quad9's resolvers, so DNS was no longer the wait. On Matthew's OK, Claude re-saved the custom domain through the API (204). GitHub's domain health check then said: pointed at a current Pages address, not the old one; eligible for HTTPS; no CAA problem; www fine. It was waiting only for GitHub to issue the certificate. Watching (Matthew's ask, 2026-10-14): a watcher in Claude's session checks every 5 minutes, for up to 24 hours, whether matthewhammer.org serves a valid certificate. When it does, Claude turns on Enforce HTTPS and finishes the ticket's remaining steps, then closes it.

PARKED 2026-10-12: measured, it would save at most about 2% of the main thread in the woods. A profiled figure move (2 runs, 4.4 and 4.1 s): Html to virtual DOM 1.1%, diff and patch 0.9%, browser layout and paint 1.4%, GC 21%, evaluating the view about 50% (about 69% with its GC), the app's own update machinery about 25%. It would also need a content hash as its key, since the woods' shapes are fresh objects each time, and handlers that find the current state at event time. The lever is evaluating the view: ^ticket(1), ^ticket(2), ^ticket(18).

closed_tickets.text: Messed Up Dress Up: music by category, and transposing by interval. (1) Categories: a small number, about 8: reggae, house, groove, waltz, calypso, classic beats, and a few more of our choosing. Every category gets at least one song, a new one where none fits yet. The 17 tunes today could seed most of them: reggae (sunny reggae, bubble reggae, turtle steppers dub), calypso (beach calypso, beach soca jump-up, steel-pan lullaby), waltz (spooky waltz), and chases (tree-house, duck-pond, round-the-house); the rest to sort. The music picker becomes two chips: song category, then track. Classic beats gets three new funk / hip-hop instrumentals in the spirit of "Apache" (Incredible Bongo Band), about 3 minutes each, with sections that feature, in turn: bass guitar, bongo drums, drum kit (funk playing), organ, and rhythm and lead guitars, so each part can be heard on its own (and on the mixing board). Our own tunes in that style (breakbeat kit, bongos, organ, twangy guitar), not Apache's melody or its break. closed_tickets.text: Merkle names at construction, then remeasure ^report(9)'s derived-names experiment. 009: content-derived names took the woods' evaluation from 1.9 s to 44.2 s. Today Util.ValueHash is a LAZY Merkle hash: a walk on first use, remembered per object in a WeakMap; TypHash (#2661) remembers types' hashes per object; nothing is hashed as it is built, and environments and closures only as generic values. Fix: compute each node's content name when it is built, from its children's names (already known), an environment frame's from its parent's and its binding, a closure's from its environment and body: a few operations per allocation, never a walk (the paper's constant cost). A content name is separate from the provenance id a step's result keeps for probes, or two values from one piece of syntax would share a name. Steps: (1) profile the derived mode first, to find where the 23x goes (walks, the WeakMap and GC, fallbacks); (2) the construction-time names; (3) remeasure gensyms, names kept and time; (4) then finish ^report(9)'s edits, including a CORRECTION: its claim that a hash that gives up is not remembered is wrong (ValueHash marks it unhashable, and a too-deep walk leaves objects marked busy for good). FOUND 2026-10-13: (a) the hashing is linear within an evaluation (each object walked once: 1,033,746 walked, 932,980 reused, the same every run); (b) but time per evaluation grew across a session (2.3 -> 5.5 -> 6.3 s; 44.2 s after a long run) with the same work and a growing heap: the side table (ValueHash's WeakMap). (c) Names kept ON each value (a hidden property, ~/.cache/hazel-diag/merkle_on_object.patch): flat, 2.2 / 2.5 / 2.2 s, about 1.4x fresh ids (1.6 s), names still kept (33,846 of 33,847). Full remeasure running.
closed_tickets.outcome: Matthew's hunch was right: the hashing was linear, but the side table it was kept in (ValueHash's WeakMap) made each evaluation slower than the last (2.3, 5.5, 6.3 s for the same work). Merkle names kept on the values (a hidden property, computed as a value is built) hold still (2.2, 2.5, 2.2 s) and cost 12 to 28% over fresh ids, not 23 times. ^report(9) updated: a section on it, two corrections, a theme-aware thumbnail. closed_tickets.text: Dress Up performance fix: dragging the friend where the cauldron's fumes turn (outside the witch's hut and inside it). The double-helix fumes make a drag slow enough to be a real UX problem. Likely why (from the code, not yet measured): every pointermove calls changed(), whose draw() replaces the whole picture (pic.innerHTML = svg); helixSvg draws each strand as short segments, about a hundred in all, each with four SMIL <animate>s on x1, x2, stroke-width and stroke-opacity, so every move re-parses them and restarts every animation, and the geometry they animate is repainted each frame. Matthew's idea: pause animations while dragging (pic.pauseAnimations() on pointerdown, unpauseAnimations() on letting go). Other ideas: draw at most once per animation frame however many pointermoves arrive; on a figure drag, move only the friend (its group's transform) and leave the scene's DOM alone, so the fumes neither restart nor re-parse; keep the scene in a group of its own that is replaced only when its settings change; make the fumes cheaper (fewer segments, or turn a group with a transform the compositor can animate). Measure first (performance before features): a drag's frame times in both scenes, before and after, against a scene without fumes. Changes go under Unreleased; no version bump or push until Matthew says.
closed_tickets.outcome: Measured, fixed, committed in kids-choice-games (3a27f9f), not deployed: it ships with the next Dress Up version, on Matthew's go-ahead. Measured in headless Chrome over the DevTools protocol (real mouse events, a 60-move drag of the friend, frames timed in the page). Before: the witch's woods took 8.1 s for the drag, frame gaps median 67 ms and p95 250 ms; inside the hut 4.2 s, p95 183 ms; the forest and the house took 2.0 s at 60 fps. The JavaScript was cheap everywhere (changed() about 2 ms); the cost was rendering. (1) draw() wiped the whole picture with innerHTML and put the cached scenery back, so the scene's 459 SMIL animations were torn out and re-registered on every move; now the scenery stays in place and the rest is replaced around it (woods 8.1 to 3.9 s). (2) The fumes cost even at rest, about 15 fps in the woods with no input; Matthew's idea, pausing the picture's animations while a drag is held, finishes it: both scenes now take 2.0 s at a steady 60 fps, like a scene without fumes.
